newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. int'l trade gap seen lower in Sept.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. int'l trade gap seen lower in Sept.

text.p: The U.S. international trade deficit likely shrank in September as imports trailed off but exports remained buoyant, analysts said.
A Reuter poll consensus forecast predicted the September trade gap narrowed to $9.5 billion from $10.83 billion in August. Data are due out Wednesday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.

"There were import duties that came off quite a bit in that month of September," said Raphael Marrone, a money market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "So, that suggests that imports were lower."

A huge inflow of holiday-related goods from China limited improvement in the August U.S. international trade gap. In fact, the U.S. bilateral trade shortfall with China ballooned 23 percent to a record $4.71 billion in that month.

"We imported a lot of Christmas merchandise...from toys to sweaters and that's why our imports from China went sky-high," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Corp. But he doubted such strong demand continued in September.
The politically sensitive trade deficit with Japan had shrunk 11.8 percent to $3.8 billion in August. This trend is seen to have continued in September.
"Our deficit with Japan will probably improve a little longer, but I don't think that's going to go on forever," said Sohn, a senior vice president at Norwest.
Sohn warned the Japanese trade surplus with the U.S. may start to rise again near-term as the Japanese yen remains weak, while the dollar continues strong.
Indeed, Japan's Ministry of Finance earlier reported that Japan's surplus with the U.S. jumped 31.3 percent in October from a year ago, its first such rise in 20 months.
The dollar traded around 111.40 yen during Monday afternoon.
The U.S. currency has battled back from a post-World War II low of 79.75 yen reached on April 19, 1995.

On the opposite side of the ledger, further improvement is expected in total U.S. exports, which rose three percent in August. "Exports probably continued to be relatively buoyant, we suspect, because our contacts in the industry suggested as much," DMG's Marrone said.
Marrone cited another positive sign in that the exports component of the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index has remained significantly above 50 for some time.
The NAPM export orders index stood at 56.1 in October, the last month for which data were available.
ASK Financial Research President Sam Kahan expects the U.S. trade gap to improve amid an increase in imports but a faster pick-up in exports.
Kahan said exports of capital goods and agricultural products should increase, while a competitive U.S. economy continues to import foreign goods.
